title: How LLM APIs work
summary: What really happens when Notely's AI summary button calls the Claude API: tokens, messages, the context window, output limits and picking a model.
youWillLearn: What a token is, and why it is the unit of cost, speed and limits
Why the API has no memory, and what the messages array is for
What the context window and max_tokens limit, and how to spot a cut-off answer
How to choose a model per feature, and where the API key must live

glossary.LLM: Large language model: a program trained on huge amounts of text that continues a piece of text by predicting what comes next.
glossary.token: A small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a word. Models read, write and bill in tokens.
glossary.system prompt: Standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the conversation, that set the model's role and rules.
glossary.messages: The list of turns in a conversation, each marked as from the user or the assistant, sent in full with every request.
glossary.context window: The maximum number of tokens a model can take in one request: instructions, conversation, documents and its own answer together.
glossary.max_tokens: A request setting that caps how many tokens the model may write in its answer. When it is hit, the answer stops mid-sentence.
glossary.stop_reason: A field in the API response that says why the model stopped: it finished, it hit max_tokens, it wants to use a tool, and so on.
glossary.temperature: A setting on many LLM APIs that controls how random the word choices are. Low is more predictable, high is more varied.
glossary.API key: A secret string that proves a request comes from your account. Anyone holding it can spend your money.

steps.title: The summary button is a black box
body: Maya opens a long note in Notely and clicks AI summary. A few seconds later, three tidy bullet points appear.

You built that with Claude Code, and it works. But if a client asks why it costs what it costs, or why long notes fail, you cannot answer yet. Everything in this module starts with what happens inside that one call.

scene.caption: The browser asks Notely's server for a summary. The server asks the Claude API. The middle of the story is unknown.

steps.title: A model guesses the next piece of text
body: An LLM does one thing: given some text, it predicts the next small piece. Then it adds that piece and predicts again, until it decides to stop.
Those pieces are tokens. A token is often a short word or part of a longer one. Your prompt goes in as tokens, and the answer comes back as tokens, one at a time.

callout.text: Your phone's autocomplete, scaled up enormously. It has read so much text that "what comes next" turns into summaries, code and answers.

scene.caption: The prompt goes in. The answer comes out one token at a time.

steps.title: Tokens are the unit of everything
body: Providers bill per token, with separate prices for input (what you send) and output (what the model writes). Output tokens usually cost several times more.

Tokens also measure speed, because the model writes one at a time, and limits, because every model has a token ceiling. So a 40-page note costs more and takes longer than a shopping list, every single click.

callout.text: Every API response includes a usage object with input and output token counts. Log it from day one. It is the only honest answer to "what does this feature cost?"

scene.caption: Every request is measured in input tokens and output tokens.

steps.title: The API has no memory
body: Each call starts from zero, like HTTP itself. The model does not remember Maya's last request.

So you send everything, every time: a system prompt with standing rules, plus a list of messages. For a chat, that list holds the whole conversation so far, and it grows with each turn. That is why long chats get slower and more expensive.

code.caption: One request: instructions, the conversation, and a cap on the answer's length.

scene.caption: The server re-sends the instructions and the whole conversation on every call.

steps.title: The context window is a desk, not a shelf
body: The context window is the most the model can look at in one request: system prompt, messages, documents and its own answer, all counted in tokens.
It is a hard limit. Send more and the API rejects the request. Even below the limit, a cluttered desk hurts: stuffing in everything "just in case" costs more and can make answers worse.

callout.text: A desk holds only what fits on it right now. Your database is the shelf. Lesson 5 is about fetching the right pages from the shelf instead of dumping all of them on the desk.

scene.caption: Everything must fit inside the context window, the answer included.

steps.title: Answers have a length cap
body: You also set max_tokens: the most the model may write. Hit it, and the answer stops mid-sentence, with no error.

Each response tells you why it ended in stop_reason. end_turn means it finished. max_tokens means it was cut off. Check it before you save the summary, or Notely will store half a bullet and look broken.

callout.text: On models that reason before they answer, that hidden thinking also counts toward max_tokens. A tight cap can cut the answer off early, so leave generous room.

code.caption: A cut-off answer still arrives with status 200. Only stop_reason tells you.

scene.caption: The answer hit max_tokens and stopped halfway. The response still says 200 OK.

steps.title: Temperature: how adventurous the words are
body: The model does not pick the single likeliest token every time. It samples. Temperature is the classic knob for that: low means predictable, high means more varied.

Many APIs still expose it. Newer Claude models have dropped it and reject requests that set it, so you steer them with clear prompts instead. Check the docs for the exact model you use before copying old snippets.

callout.text: Even with the most predictable settings, the same prompt can give different answers. Never build a feature that needs the exact same words twice. Lesson 7 shows how to test features that vary.

scene.caption: Same note, two clicks, two slightly different summaries.

steps.title: Pick a model per feature
body: Providers sell model families in sizes. Small models are fast and cheap. Large ones reason better but are slower and cost more.

Choose per feature, not per app. Notely's one-paragraph summary runs fine on a small model. A "plan my week from 200 notes" feature may need a large one. Keep the model id in an env var, so you can switch without a code change.

callout.text: Ask: which model is each feature using, and why? Is the model id in an env var or hard-coded in five files? Is max_tokens set and stop_reason checked? Is usage logged? Model names change often, so ask Claude Code to check the provider's current model list.

scene.caption: One app, several models: pick the smallest one that does each job well.

steps.title: The API key stays on the server
body: The API key pays for every token. If it reaches the browser, anyone can copy it from the JavaScript bundle and run their own app on your bill.

The classic slip: an env var named NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. That prefix tells Next.js to ship the value to every visitor. The browser should call your route, and only your route calls the model.

callout.text: Leaked keys get found by bots within hours of a public push. If one leaks, rotate it in the provider console right away, then check the usage page.

scene.caption: A key in browser code is a key for everyone. Keep it in a server-only env var.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: An LLM predicts the next token, over and over. Tokens are what you pay for, wait for, and run out of.

The API remembers nothing, so every call carries the system prompt and the full message list, and all of it must fit in the context window. Cap the answer with max_tokens, check stop_reason, pick the smallest model that works, and keep the key on the server.

quiz.question: Notely's chat feature gets slower and more expensive the longer Maya chats. Why?

options.text: The model gets tired after many messages.
options.why: Models have no state between calls. Nothing about the model changes during a chat.

options.text: Each request re-sends the whole conversation, so input tokens grow every turn.
options.why: The API has no memory. The messages array carries the full history, so every turn adds tokens to every later call.

options.text: The provider charges a fee per message, rising over time.
options.why: Billing is per token, not per message. The cost grows because the token count grows.

quiz.question: Some saved summaries end mid-sentence, but the logs show only 200 OK responses. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The database column is too short.
options.why: Possible in theory, but the classic cause is the model's cap. Check the response before blaming storage.

options.text: The network dropped the end of the response.
options.why: A dropped connection usually shows up as an error, not as a clean 200 with a shorter body.

options.text: The answer hit max_tokens; stop_reason would say so.
options.why: Hitting the output cap is not an error. The response is a normal 200, and only stop_reason: "max_tokens" reveals the cut.

quiz.question: Claude Code put NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env so a React component can call the Claude API directly. What do you ask for?

options.text: Rename it without the prefix and move the call into a server route the component calls.
options.why: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix bundles the value into browser code. Server-only env vars plus your own route keep the key secret.

options.text: Keep it, but minify the JavaScript so the key is hard to find.
options.why: Minifying does not hide strings. Anyone can open dev tools and find the key in seconds.

options.text: Keep it, since the repository is private.
options.why: The repo being private does not matter. The key ships to every visitor's browser at runtime.

takeaways: An LLM writes one token at a time. Tokens are the unit of cost, speed and limits.
The API has no memory: every call sends the system prompt and the full messages list.
Everything, including the answer, must fit in the context window. More context is not always better.
Set max_tokens and check stop_reason: a cut-off answer still returns 200.
Pick the smallest model that does each job well, keep its id in an env var, and keep the API key server-side.
